title: Food tests and chromatography; Plant transport: xylem and transpiration
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BM09a#t4 term and clue written for the game; BM09a#t3 term and clue written for the game; BM09b#t1 term and clue written for the game; BM09a#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM09a#N.4a, BM09b#N.4, EX10a#N.2, BM09a#N.10, EX10a#N.7, BM09a#N.14, EX10a#N.11, EX10a#N.12a.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Reducing sugars
items.clue: Group made up of all monosaccharides plus maltose and lactose

items.label: Biuret test
items.clue: A change from blue to lilac shows that peptide bonds are present

items.label: Stationary phase
items.clue: The paper, or a thin layer of silica gel on a plate, which stays put

items.label: Iodine test
items.clue: A change from orange-brown to blue-black shows that starch is present

questions.stem: A solution gives a negative result with iodine. With Benedict's reagent, heated, it stays blue. A fresh sample is boiled with dilute hydrochloric acid, neutralised, and tested with Benedict's again: a brick-red precipitate forms. What does the solution contain?

options.text: A reducing sugar, because the final Benedict's test was positive.
Starch, which the acid broke down into glucose.
A non-reducing sugar, such as sucrose, and no reducing sugar.
A reducing sugar made by the acid joining smaller sugars by condensation.

questions.explanation: Negative first, positive after acid hydrolysis: the acid split a non-reducing sugar into reducing monosaccharides.

questions.stem: On a paper chromatogram of leaf pigments, the origin line was 20 mm from the bottom edge of the paper, the centre of the carotene spot was 65 mm from the bottom edge and the solvent front was 70 mm from the bottom edge. What is the Rf value of carotene?
questions.explanation: From the origin, the pigment moved 65 − 20 = 45 mm and the solvent front 70 − 20 = 50 mm. Rf = 45 ÷ 50 = 0.90.

questions.stem: Why is transpiration described as a consequence of gas exchange rather than as a process the leaf carries out for its own sake?

options.text: The plant opens its stomata in order to lose water, because transpiration is needed to pull water up through the xylem.
Stomata must be open for carbon dioxide to enter, and water vapour inevitably diffuses out through the same pores.
Water vapour escapes across the cuticle and epidermis wherever gases are exchanged over the leaf surface.
Transpiration is evaporation that depends only on temperature, so it happens whether or not the stomata are open.

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis requires carbon dioxide, which can only enter through open stomata. While they are open, water vapour from the saturated air spaces diffuses out down its concentration gradient to the drier atmosphere; the water loss is an unavoidable side effect of gas exchange.

questions.stem: You have a 10.0 mmol dm⁻³ glucose stock solution. How do you make 10.0 cm³ of a 4.0 mmol dm⁻³ standard?

options.text: 4.0 cm³ of stock + 10.0 cm³ of water
4.0 cm³ of stock + 6.0 cm³ of water
6.0 cm³ of stock + 4.0 cm³ of water
0.40 cm³ of stock + 9.6 cm³ of water

questions.explanation: You need 4.0 ÷ 10.0 = 0.40 of the final volume as stock: 0.40 × 10.0 = 4.0 cm³, made up to 10.0 cm³ with 6.0 cm³ of water.

questions.stem: Why are the walls of xylem vessels thickened with lignin?

options.text: To seal the vessel completely so that no water can escape through the side walls into surrounding cells.
To provide the mitochondria and cytoplasm of the vessel with a surface on which to generate ATP for transport.
To hold the plant upright, which is the only function that lignin has anywhere in the xylem.
To withstand the tension in the water column so that the vessel is not pulled inwards and collapsed.

questions.explanation: The negative pressure potential generated by transpiration would suck a soft-walled tube flat. Lignified walls are rigid enough to withstand these tensions, keeping the vessel open for unimpeded flow; they also contribute to supporting the plant.

questions.stem: A sample of milk is tested. Heated with Benedict's reagent: an orange-red precipitate. With biuret reagent: lilac. With iodine in potassium iodide: stays orange-brown. Which conclusion is supported?

options.text: It contains glucose and no other sugar.
It contains starch, protein and a reducing sugar.
It contains a reducing sugar and protein, but no detectable lipid.
It contains a reducing sugar and protein, but no detectable starch.

questions.explanation: Precipitate: reducing sugar. Lilac: peptide bonds, so protein. No blue-black: no starch detected.

questions.stem: What generates the force that draws water up the xylem from the roots to the leaves?

options.text: Cells in the root pump water into the base of the xylem, pushing the whole column up to the leaves.
Evaporation of water from leaf cell walls draws water out of the xylem, putting the water column under tension.
The living xylem cells use ATP from respiration to move water molecules upwards against gravity.
Water evaporates from the open ends of the xylem vessels at the leaf surface, sucking the column up.

questions.explanation: Loss of water by transpiration from the cell walls of leaf cells causes water to be drawn out of the xylem vessels and through cell walls by capillary action. This generates tension, a negative pressure potential, and it is this tension that draws water up the xylem.

questions.stem: Florists cut the stems of fresh flowers under water. A stem cut in air and then put in a vase often wilts, even though its cut end is in water. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Cutting the stem removes the roots, which were pumping water up to the flowers, so the flow stops.
Water in the xylem is under positive pressure, so it pours out of the cut end and the stem empties.
Cutting kills the xylem cells, so they can no longer use ATP to move water up the stem.
Xylem water is under tension, so air is drawn into the cut vessels and breaks the columns.
